tldr: In a spring-loaded monopod hopping robot with pitch unlocked, this study proposes a new control method that actively uses the hip reaction torque from pitch stabilization to counteract damping losses and drive forward acceleration, demonstrating fast, stable hopping up to 8.85 leg lengths/s (1.77 m/s) on physical hardware.
hero_caption: Two robot platforms evaluated in this study. (A) is the physical "Penn Jerboa" equipped with a 2-DOF tail and compliant spring legs, and (B) is a generic planar 5-link biped used in simulation. Both run primarily driven by hip joint torques.
overview:
While legged robots are gaining higher mobility, conventional designs that pack multiple actuators into each leg run into strict limits on weight and power consumption. How can we convert high-density power into propulsion using fewer actuators? This paper focuses on an extreme underactuated model: a pitch-unlocked 3-DOF SLIP model with passive compliant legs driven solely at the hip joints.

The authors came up with a counterintuitive idea: use the very torque needed for pitch stabilization as the primary energy source for forward running and hopping. When the center of mass (COM) is intentionally offset forward from directly above the hip joint, keeping body pitch upright demands a large steady reaction torque at the hip. This torque injects propulsion energy into the gait through the leg. However, continuously driving the hip accelerates only the leg's rotational velocity, draining energy from the leg's radial extension and eventually causing hopping to fail. To solve this, the authors introduced a novel stepping policy with intentionally asymmetric touchdown and liftoff angles, establishing a mechanism that channels excess angular energy back into radial leg extension (hopping).

Mathematically, the authors extended hybrid averaging analysis to derive exact, closed-form analytical solutions for the fixed points and local stability (eigenvalues) of the resulting limit cycles, despite the nonlinear hybrid dynamics. They then validated the framework through simulations and physical experiments on a tailed robot, the "Penn Jerboa."

The results showed that the analytical predictions matched the simulations and hardware experiments with only about 6 to 16% error. On the physical robot, the system achieved exceptionally fast continuous hopping at speeds between 1.02 m/s and 1.77 m/s (5.10 to 8.85 leg lengths/s).
contributions: Proposed a hip-energized SLIP control strategy that recruits pitch stabilization torque to inject and replenish propulsion and hopping energy
Theoretically and mathematically proved that an asymmetric stepping policy is essential for redistributing hip-injected angular energy into radial hopping energy
Extended hybrid averaging analysis to a 2-DOF SLIP system, deriving closed-form expressions for periodic orbit fixed points and eigenvalues in a non-integrable system
Demonstrated fast, stable hopping up to 8.85 leg lengths/s on the physical tailed robot Penn Jerboa, showing close agreement with both simulation and analytical predictions

sections.heading: Why hop using only the hip? The challenge of underactuated robotics
sections.summary: In contrast to current trends of cramming high-power, multi-DOF actuators into every leg, this work explores running by maximizing power from a minimal set of actuators. It highlights the importance of a new controller that injects hopping energy via hip torque while stabilizing pitch, supported by mathematical analysis.
sections.details:
In recent years, quadrupeds and bipeds have achieved high agility using three or more actuators per leg governed by sophisticated COM dynamics control. However, given actuator power-to-weight limits, one must wonder: does every leg really need that many actuators, or can alternative designs and control strategies extract maximum performance from far fewer driven joints?

The Penn Jerboa studied in this paper (Fig. F1-A) has only one motor per leg at the hip, leaving the leg itself as a passive spring. Prior work tried to pump energy into the leg springs by vigorously pitching a 2-DOF tail. In contrast, this paper tackles the challenge: can we achieve stable, high-speed sagittal locomotion driven purely by hip joint torque?

In earlier literature, numerical simulations explored SLIP (Spring-Loaded Inverted Pendulum) control strategies targeting a Virtual Pivot Point (VPP) or maintaining mean angular momentum. However, pitch stabilization coupled with hip-torque-induced hopping had never been demonstrated on physical hardware.

This study leverages hybrid averaging analysis to analytically derive fixed points and stability, proving its effectiveness through both simulations (a planar 5-link biped and the Jerboa) and physical hardware experiments.

captions.F1: Validation platforms used in this study. (A) is the physical "Penn Jerboa" with passive compliant legs and a 2-DOF tail, and (B) is a planar 5-link biped model used for simulation.

sections.heading: Mathematical analysis: Cascade decomposition and the necessity of asymmetric stepping
sections.summary: By decoupling the 3-DOF SLIP model into a cascade of a pitch system and a translational SLIP system, closed-form periodic solutions were derived via hybrid averaging. The authors proved that an asymmetric touchdown stepping policy is mathematically required to sustain hip-driven energy injection.
sections.details:
The core of the model and analysis lies in viewing the pitch-unlocked 3-DOF SLIP system (Fig. F2) as a cascade: an independent 1-DOF pitch subsystem driving a perturbed 2-DOF translational SLIP subsystem.

- **Pitch stabilization and energy injection (Sections 2.1–2.2)**: The center of mass (COM) is offset horizontally from the hip by $d_x$. During stance, a PD + feedforward controller (Eq. 2) regulating pitch to a target $\phi^d$ produces a large steady torque $ ar{	au}$ to counter the moment about the COM. This reaction torque performs work on the translational system, offsetting damping losses. The pitch subsystem uses an integral-like discrete torque-bias update (Eq. 4), guaranteeing LTI stability (Proposition 1).

- **New coordinates and averaging (Section 2.3)**: Although the translational SLIP system is non-integrable, the authors introduced "spherical-like" state variables (Eq. 14): total mechanical energy $a_e$ (in velocity units $\mathrm{m/s}$), an "Energy Ratio" $\psi_e$ representing the velocity component normal to the leg, and radial phase $\psi_r$. Applying hybrid averaging yielded explicit expressions for the averaged dynamics (Proposition 2).

- **Necessity of an asymmetric stepping policy (Theorem 2)**: This produces a crucial physical insight. Hip torque accelerates only the leg angular velocity $\dot{	heta}$; unmanaged, angular energy diverges while radial hopping energy drops to zero. To prevent this, the controller uses an asymmetric stepping policy (Eq. 22) that intentionally offsets the touchdown angle $	heta_{	ext{td}}$ relative to the liftoff angle $	heta_{	ext{lo}}$. Using the touchdown reset map to channel angular energy into radial extension stably balances fore-aft speed and apex height.

captions.F2: Cascade decomposition of the 3-DOF SLIP system. The 1-DOF pitch system in (A) energizes the 2-DOF translational SLIP system in (B) via hip torque $\tau$, making mathematical analysis tractable.

sections.heading: Deploying to hardware: Broadening the basin of attraction
sections.summary: To implement the theoretical controller on simulated and physical systems subject to initial condition variability (such as hand tosses), the authors added a discrete energy controller and a liftoff energy ratio estimation algorithm.
sections.details:
Directly applying elegant theoretical control laws to realistic simulations or the physical Jerboa can lead to failure when initial conditions deviate. Because hardware runs start from a gentle manual toss, the controller requires a wide basin of attraction to tolerate scattered starting states.

- **Adjusting COM offset (Section 3.1)**: In the 5-link biped, changing the torso pitch angle geometrically shifts the COM offset $d_x$. On the tailed Jerboa, pitching the tail upward directly shifts the COM offset $d_x$ relative to the hip.

- **Discrete energy control and feedforward (Section 3.2)**: To prevent energy loss when a hand toss lacks sufficient momentum, a discrete PD controller (Eq. 36) updates $d_x$ step-to-step based on apex energy error. Combining this with a feedforward torque estimate initialized from $d_x$ (Eq. 37) substantially improved convergence.

- **Energy ratio estimation (Section 3.3)**: While theory uses the liftoff energy ratio $\psi_e$ to set the next touchdown angle, hardware liftoff detection delays of just a few milliseconds cause the foot to spin in the air, creating sharp spikes in velocity ratios. Estimating $\hat{\psi}_e$ (Eq. 38) from average mid-stance velocity and feeding it to the stepping policy provided robust noise tolerance.

sections.heading: Simulation results: Accurate predictions and an emergent VPP
sections.summary: Tests on the planar 5-link biped and Jerboa in Gazebo confirmed a 4-fold energy control range via COM offset. Averaged fixed-point predictions matched actual speed and height within 6 to 14% error.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted in realistic Gazebo simulations with a 1 kHz control loop and 100 g unsprung foot masses.

- **Energy regulation capacity (Section 4.1)**: Adjusting the COM offset $d_x$ (via tail angle or torso lean) enabled continuous tuning of steady-state hopping energy across a 4-fold range in Joules (roughly a 2-fold range in speed).

- **Steady-state trajectory behavior (Section 4.2)**: As shown in the time-series data of Fig. 7, the stance-averaged hip torque $ ar{	au}$ fluctuated by less than 1% step-to-step, and the energy ratio converged smoothly near its target. Clear asymmetry between touchdown and liftoff angles emerged exactly as predicted by theory.

- **Fixed-point prediction accuracy (Section 4.3)**: Comparing theoretical closed-form predictions (Eq. 30) against simulation outcomes (Table 9) revealed an average error of only 13.8% for forward speed and 6.5% for apex height. Although errors increased slightly at higher energy levels due to mild assumption violations, the analytical model captured performance trends remarkably well.

- **Emergence of a Virtual Pivot Point (Section 4.4)**: Ground reaction force vectors naturally intersected at a single point above the body—the Virtual Pivot Point (VPP) observed in animal running. Even without any explicit VPP-targeting terms in the controller, VPP behavior emerged spontaneously from pitch stabilization and asymmetric stepping, offering a compelling biomechanical insight.

sections.heading: Physical experiments: Fast hopping demonstrated on the Penn Jerboa
sections.summary: Using the boom-mounted Jerboa robot, the team achieved stable, continuous hopping between 1.02 and 1.77 m/s (up to 8.85 leg lengths/s), validating the theoretical model's qualitative and quantitative accuracy amid real-world nonlinearities.
sections.details:
Following simulations, sagittal running experiments were carried out on the physical "Penn Jerboa" constrained to a 2 m radius boom.

- **Hardware challenges and control robustness (Sections 5.1–5.2)**: The physical robot legs are not simple linear springs; they use a 4-bar linkage with extension springs. This introduces nonlinear stiffness and parasitic fore-aft forces during leg compression. The system also faced boom roll backlash causing timing offsets between bilateral feet, alongside encoder noise. Despite these disturbances, hip torque control combined with the asymmetric stepping policy functioned stably, enabling indefinite, continuous hopping without falls.

- **Locomotion performance and model accuracy (Section 5.3)**: Forward speeds reached 1.02 m/s to 1.77 m/s, translating to an impressive scale-adjusted speed of 5.10 to 8.85 leg lengths/s. Comparison with the analytical model (Table 10) showed average errors of 16.4% in forward speed and 12.1% in apex height, proving that the theoretical predictions retain practical accuracy even under severe physical disturbances.

sections.heading: Discussion and conclusion: The deep link between posture and energy
sections.summary: The proposed strategy dramatically outperformed earlier tail-energized methods (which peaked at 1.0 m/s and failed after 20 steps). The insight linking COM offset, pitch torque, and stepping asymmetry offers valuable principles for general biped and quadruped design and MPC.
sections.details:
The authors provide a multi-faceted discussion on the implications and future directions of this work.

- **Comparison with prior methods (Section 6.7)**: Previous experiments on the same Jerboa platform (Shamsah et al., 2018) energized the legs by pitching the tail, reaching only 0.2 to 1.0 m/s and lasting at most 20 steps before falling. The proposed method nearly doubles the running speed and sustains continuous running without falling, marking a major leap in capability.

- **Posture, energy, and the essence of asymmetry (Sections 6.3–6.4)**: The core takeaways—that an off-hip COM demands a pitch-stabilizing hip torque that inevitably accelerates the system, and that an asymmetric stepping policy is mathematically required to redirect this energy into hopping—extend far beyond monopeds. In model predictive control (MPC) for heavy-load humanoids or rapidly accelerating quadrupeds, stepping controllers should explicitly allow and optimize asymmetric gaits rather than enforcing artificial symmetry.

- **Future work**: Because the current platform is mechanically constrained to the sagittal plane by a boom, future work will integrate roll-axis stabilization to achieve fully autonomous 3D hopping.

takeaways: The hip reaction torque exerted to stabilize body pitch can serve directly as the primary energy source for forward propulsion and hopping
The problem of excess leg rotational energy caused by hip torque can be resolved by an asymmetric stepping policy, redirecting energy back into radial leg extension (hopping)
Hybrid averaging analysis enables closed-form mathematical predictions of limit cycle fixed points and stability boundaries even in non-integrable spring-legged hopping systems
In optimization problems like MPC, permitting deliberate touchdown asymmetry rather than forcing symmetric gaits is key to unlocking greater agility
limitations: The robot cannot start hopping from a dead stop on its own; it requires a manual toss by an operator to initiate running
Experimental validation is restricted to sagittal-plane motion via a boom constraint; fully autonomous 3D running with roll and yaw remains unverified
The analytical model relies on approximations (such as small angle and low damping assumptions in Tables 3–5), causing prediction errors to grow at extreme speeds and energy levels
